paragraphs.text: Torsion dystonia is a movement disorder in which control of voluntary movements is lost. It appears as sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that often cause twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures (Ozelius et al., 1989; Kwiatkowski et al., 1991). In the early-onset form, these twisting muscle contractures begin in childhood, and the symptoms are believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia (Ozelius et al., 1997). Most familial forms are transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance and variable expressivity (Ozelius et al., 1989; Kwiatkowski et al., 1991). The GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but only 30% of mutation carriers develop the disease (Risch et al., 2007).

paragraphs.text: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) studied the brains of 2 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans after death. They found no important histologic changes in the basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, higher brainstem nuclei, locus ceruleus, or raphe nuclei. Norepinephrine was markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Serotonin was subnormal in the dorsal raphe nucleus, and dopamine was subnormal in the nucleus accumbens and, in 1 of the 2 cases, in the striatum. Norepinephrine was raised in the septum, thalamus, colliculi, red nucleus, and dorsal raphe nucleus, and serotonin was elevated in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Homovanillic acid levels showed little consistent change. The authors suggested that a disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms may be a basic neurochemical abnormality in the disorder.

paragraphs.text: McNaught et al. (2004) studied 4 clinically documented and genetically confirmed DYT1 patients at autopsy. No inclusion bodies were detected in the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatum, hippocampus, or selected regions of the cerebral cortex. paragraphs.text: In a man with late-onset oromandibular dystonia beginning in his fifth decade, Calakos et al. (2010) identified a heterozygous c.613T-A change in exon 3 of the TOR1A gene, resulting in a phe205-to-ile (F205I) substitution at a highly conserved residue in the AAA domain.
